newsitem.title: USA: House panel votes to nullify Clinton Mexico ruling.
newsitem.headline: House panel votes to nullify Clinton Mexico ruling.

text.p: A House of Representatives committee voted on Thursday to overturn President Bill Clinton's finding that Mexico is fully cooperating in the anti-drug war but to waive imposition of sanctions against the Mexican government.
Over administration objections, the International Relations Committee voted 27-5 to send the measure to the full House for action. Similar legislation has been introduced in the Senate.

Under a 1961 law congressional disapproval of Clinton's certification last Friday that Mexico is an anti-drug ally automatically triggers a ban on U.S. aid and requires votes against multilateral development bank assistance to Mexico.
But the panel and many members of Congress are unwilling to go that far, fearing such action might provoke Mexico to cut off all cooperation in the fight against drug trafficking.

"The president made the wrong decision and this resolution sets the record straight while preserving appropriate stability in our relationship with Mexico," Chairman Benjamin Gilman, a New York Republican, said.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright criticised the Congressional action and insisted that Mexico was making progress in its drug fight.
"This is not a blame game. It is an attempt to deal with a problem that is bad for Mexico and bad for the United States," she said on the PBS programme "Newshour with Jim Lehrer."
Albright praised President Ernesto Zedillo for his "high level of cooperation," saying the Mexican leader knew he had "a big job" but was committed to dealing with it.

Mexican drug cartels control much of the U.S.-bound cocaine traffic and congressional calls for decertification of Mexico intensified after the leading Mexican official in the anti-drug fight, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, was arrested on charges of taking bribes from a drug kingpin.

Administration officials at the House committee meeting also spoke of positive trends and a dramatic increase in cooperation in Mexico, but a high-ranking Drug Enforcement Administration official, James Milford, said: "We do not have an open relationship with Mexican law enforcement."
Milford said information that had been passed to Mexican authorities had often been compromised.

Rep Lee Hamilton, an Indiana Democrat, said he was giving "tentative" support to the committee resolution. He said the 1961 law should be repealed because it forced the administration to make a choice between a "good" or "bad" finding and caused difficulties in U.S. foreign relations.

Rep Robert Menendez, a New Jersey Democrat, said the certification process was regarded in other countries as an issue of national sovereignty, particularly in Latin America, where it was seen as interventionist.
